text: Hello, hello, and welcome to Story Nori. You're listening to Jana, and I'm back with a chilly birdie story. Birdie and the ski slopes. Jake woke up to see little flakes of snow falling outside his window. The garden was glistening and white. Great, he thought. I think I'll build a snowman. But sadly, this was not to be. In England, snow doesn't settle very often. By the time his mother was driving him to school, all the snow had turned to slushy mush. But she had surprisingly good news for him that cheered him up immensely. And he couldn't wait for the school day to end, so he could rush home to tell Birdie. That evening, a slightly shivering Birdie tapped at Jake's window. Jake opened up and quickly let Birdie in, along with a gush of freezing air. Birdie! He said excitedly. I've got great news. Mum says we're going skiing at half-turn with Uncle Jim. Can you come too? The mountain we're going to ski down is called the Pyrenees. Mum said the place is called Andorra. You could fly there, couldn't you? I could if I had the time. Oh, go on Birdie. It'll be much more fun with you there. I'll see what I can do, Birdie said. When Jake went downstairs, he asked, Mum, is skiing easy? Like everything in life, it's about practice. Your Uncle Jim and I went on our fair share of skiing holidays back when we were kids. I haven't been skiing for years, but I expect I'll soon get my ski legs back. Dad's never been skiing before, so he'll be learning with you on the baby slopes. Jake chuckled as he imagined Dad wobbling about on his skis. Jake waited and waited for half-term through long, sleepy school lessons full of kids sniffling and coughing. And at last, half-term finally came around. Au revoir, Britain. Bye-bye, grey skies. The family flew off to join Uncle Jim. He had rented a luxurious, cosy chalet, large enough for both families, with stunning views of the crisp, bright ski slopes. After breakfast the next morning, they met their ski instructor, Pierre, who had a moustache that looked like a fluffy caterpillar. First, we learned the basics. Put on your boots and then clip into your skis like this. He demonstrated by lining up the toe of his boot with the binding and pressing down with a satisfying click. Jake tried to copy him, but his first attempt ended with him toppling sideways into the snow. It's harder than it looks. He grumbled, brushing snow off his jacket. Dad, meanwhile, looked like a baby giraffe trying to stand for the first time, his legs wobbling in every direction. Pierre called out. Bend your knees, lean forward, not back. You must feel the front of your boots. After a few practice runs on a gentle slope, Pierre announced, Now we try the ski lift. Great, we're going up in the world, said Dad, which was his idea of a joke. As they ascended, Jake gazed down at the sparkling snow below. It was hard to imagine that his dreary old school even existed. After the lesson, they headed to a steeper slope to see how the experts were getting on. Mum, Uncle Jim and Cousin Roddy were due to come down soon. I hope Mum doesn't break her leg, said Elle. Uncle Jim says she's a natural, like a swan on snow, said Dad. Jake and Elle stood at the bottom of the slope, trying to spot Mum among all the brightly clothed skiers, who were expertly sliding down the slope. There she is! shrieked Elle, spotting Mum's ski suit. She looks so small up there. I hope she's not nervous. As it happened, Mum glided down the slope with smooth, controlled turns. Her skis carving elegant S-shapes into the snow. Even Pierre gave a nod of approval. Whoa! said Jake, amazed. She's actually good! Told you, like a swan on snow, said Dad. Mum reached the bottom and came to a graceful stop, sending up a small spray of snow. She pulled off her goggles and smiled. Piece of cake! I didn't know you could do that! said Elle, proudly grinning from ear to ear. Well, it's like riding a bike, said Mum, brushing snow off her jacket. You never forget. The next day, Uncle Jim announced he was taking Mum off-piste, meaning they'd ski on untouched snow, away from the main trails. Your Mum's too good for these boring old slopes, he said. We'll go exploring. Oh, be careful, Mummy. Don't get caught in an avalanche, said Elle. I promise I'll be careful, reassured Mum. Uncle Jim will be looking after me, so don't worry about a thing. Make sure you look after her, Jim. We don't want her getting lost, said Aunty Sue, Jim's wife, who was planning to go designer shopping, which she maintained was how sensible people spent the time in Andorra. The kids' skiing lesson was fun, and afterwards, Dad took them for lunch in town. They had chocolate fondue. When they got back, they were all happily exhausted, and so went to bed for a nap. When Jake woke up later that afternoon, he found Dad in the living room. I'm worried, Jake. Mum's not back, and I can't get hold of her on the phone. Don't worry, Dad, consoled Jake. She'll be fine. Well, I don't know, said Uncle Jim anxiously. I seem to lose her along the way. Lose her? asked Jake. Uncle Jim began explaining, while rubbing the back of his neck nervously. We were skiing along this beautiful stretch of untouched snow, and Lucy, that's Jake's mum, was skiing better than I expected. Before I knew it, she disappeared behind a ridge. Didn't you go after her? Dad asked, his voice tight with worry. Course I did, Uncle Jim exclaimed.
